source_text: As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, experts have an increasingly dismal assessment of his second administration. “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” said pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher . “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” Trump’s approval rating was already low, but his latest drop is among the sharpest declines of either of his terms. It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely of his own making. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump hasn’t exactly delivered on that, famously making obtuse statements like “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30 ” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. And with gas prices spiking up to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are not happy with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

source_text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating plunges to a historic low of 36 percent, the political establishment is presenting the second administration as a disaster—and using carefully selected numbers to reinforce that conclusion. Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher declared, “This is what a crater looks like in politics,” adding, “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.” But the figures are not merely reporting public opinion; they are helping manufacture the narrative, with Trump’s latest drop portrayed as one of the sharpest declines of either term. The timing comes as he faces a series of crises that opponents largely attribute to him.

The first is the economy, where public frustration has become useful material for those seeking to discredit Trump. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern—its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed after COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation, a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump, convinced his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. Those expectations have not materialized. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living.

“It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump has not delivered on that promise, instead making obtuse statements such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs.

More revealing still, gas prices approaching record highs are being used to link the condition of the Trump economy to the second major reason Americans are supposedly turning against the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground.

With gas prices spiking to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are being directed to see the consequences of Trump’s military “excursion” at the pump. Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not accepting that official line.

source_text: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big screen isn’t gone yet Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years. The closure adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue, as the movie-going scene continues to change with streaming platforms and shifting audience habits. Still, new operators like Filmhouse taking over The Projector and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that the big screen experience isn’t gone yet, even if it doesn’t look the same as before. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

source_text: Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, after more than 30 years in operation. The closure adds to the gradual reduction of Singapore’s cinema landscape, and it will be one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years, following Shaw Seletar, several Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue. Golden Village attributes the decision to streaming platforms and changing audience habits, but that explanation leaves broader questions about how much of the transformation is being driven by audiences, operators, or commercial pressures—and whose interests are served as theatres disappear. The big screen has not disappeared altogether: Filmhouse has taken over The Projector, and around 30 cinema locations are still operating islandwide. Still, those figures offer only a partial picture of what remains, and whether it resembles the cinema experience that existed before. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

source_text:
Softcare reported that revenue rose 25% last year and profit increased 27%, figures presented as another closely managed success story as the Chinese diaper maker expands across emerging markets.

The company reported 25% revenue growth, led by a 134% increase in Latin America and double-digit growth in its core African markets. Those results position Softcare at the front of a new wave of Chinese companies targeting African consumers, although the figures alone do not establish how closely that expansion aligns with a broader institutional push or what its full motives may be.

Known as the “African diaper king,” Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) has so far overcome skepticism about whether it could preserve its dominant position in Africa while extending it into other emerging markets. After the release of its first annual results late last week, the company’s newer supporters pushed its shares nearly 15% higher over the following two trading days—movement presented as a spontaneous vote of confidence, though the market reaction does not by itself verify the company’s longer-term prospects.

Softcare said revenue increased 24.9% year over year to $567 million last year, while net profit rose 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also increased from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025, a further indicator cited in support of the company’s performance.

Sales in its core African markets rose 22.5% to $545 million. Softcare is also moving beyond Africa, with its expansion into other emerging markets being characterized as a success. In Latin America, sales more than doubled to $22 million, five years after the company entered Peru in 2020 and added El Salvador in 2024. The company is also establishing a presence in Central Asia, where sales remained very small but more than doubled last year to $272,000.

After several years of declines, the average selling prices (ASP) for Softcare’s two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper ASPs increased 4.4% year over year, with that segment accounting for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product ASPs rose 7% and represented 17.5% of revenue.

The price increases support the claim that Softcare has persuaded consumers in highly price-sensitive markets to pay more, thereby protecting and even increasing its margins. The reported figures, however, do not establish whether the changes reflect stronger consumer demand or other forms of market management, and the company’s account does not address who benefits from the trend.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024, down from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.
